title: Tenerife runway collision (KLM 4805 / Pan Am 1736)

agencies.name: Comisión de Investigación de Accidentes e Incidentes de Aviación Civil
agencies.report_title: Report on the collision between KLM Boeing 747 PH-BUF and Pan Am Boeing 747 N736PA at Los Rodeos Airport, Tenerife, on 27 March 1977

summary: Both 747s had diverted to Los Rodeos after a bomb explosion closed Las Palmas. In fog, with no ground radar, the KLM aircraft backtracked runway 30 and turned for departure while the Pan Am 747 was still taxiing along the same runway looking for its exit. The KLM captain began the takeoff roll without a takeoff clearance; a simultaneous radio transmission from Pan Am and the tower blocked the warning that Pan Am was still on the runway. The KLM aircraft struck the Pan Am 747 at about 140 kt; all 248 on the KLM aircraft and 335 of the 396 on the Pan Am aircraft were killed.
probable_cause: The fundamental cause was that the KLM captain took off without clearance, did not obey the tower's 'stand by for takeoff' instruction, did not interrupt takeoff on learning that the Pan Am aircraft was still on the runway, and in reply to the flight engineer's query as to whether the Pan Am aircraft had left the runway, replied emphatically in the affirmative. Contributing factors were the fog reducing visibility below the minimum for the airport to see the runway, the simultaneous radio transmissions that made the Pan Am position report inaudible in the KLM cockpit, the use of non-standard phraseology by the KLM co-pilot and the tower, the Pan Am aircraft's failure to leave the runway at the third taxiway as instructed, and the pressure on the KLM crew from duty-time limits.

factors.evidence: The KLM captain advanced the throttles and began the takeoff roll after receiving only the route clearance, before any takeoff clearance had been issued.

Non-standard phraseology ('we are now at takeoff', 'OK... stand by for takeoff') and a simultaneous transmission from Pan Am blocked the tower's instruction and Pan Am's report that it was still on the runway.
Fog reduced visibility on the runway to about 300 m, so neither crew nor the tower could see the other aircraft.
The KLM flight engineer's question whether Pan Am was clear of the runway was dismissed by the captain, and the first officer did not challenge the takeoff.
Los Rodeos had no ground surveillance radar, so the tower could not monitor the positions of the two aircraft on the runway.
The airport was congested with diverted aircraft, taxiway lighting was unserviceable, and the taxiway exits were poorly identified in the fog.
The KLM captain was under pressure from strict Dutch duty-time regulations that threatened the crew's ability to complete the return flight.
The Pan Am crew missed the third taxiway exit they had been instructed to take and continued along the runway toward the fourth.
A small tower staff was handling many diverted aircraft in poor visibility on a single frequency.
The Pan Am 747 was still backtracking on the active runway when the KLM aircraft began its takeoff.
The KLM 747, having rotated early and struck its tail on the runway, hit the Pan Am fuselage at about 140 kt and crashed back onto the runway in flames.
Both aircraft were destroyed by fire; all 248 on the KLM aircraft died and only 61 of the Pan Am occupants survived.

events.text: A bomb explosion at Las Palmas closes the airport; KLM 4805 and Pan Am 1736 are among many aircraft diverted to Los Rodeos, which becomes congested.
Las Palmas reopens; the KLM captain decides to refuel fully at Tenerife, delaying departure and blocking the Pan Am aircraft on the apron. Duty-time limits concern the KLM crew.
Tower instructs KLM to backtrack runway 30 and make a 180 degree turn at the end; fog is rolling across the airfield and visibility is falling.
Pan Am is instructed to backtrack the runway and leave it at the third taxiway; the crew are unsure which exit is the third and continue past it.
KLM completes its turn at the end of runway 30 and lines up; the captain begins to advance the throttles and the first officer says they do not yet have ATC clearance.
Tower issues the route clearance (not a takeoff clearance); the KLM first officer reads it back ending with 'we are now at takeoff'.
The KLM captain releases the brakes and begins the takeoff roll without clearance.

Tower replies 'OK... stand by for takeoff, I will call you'; simultaneously Pan Am transmits 'we are still taxiing down the runway'. The two transmissions overlap and only a squeal is heard in the KLM cockpit.
KLM flight engineer asks whether Pan Am is clear of the runway; the captain replies emphatically yes and continues the takeoff.
Pan Am crew see the KLM landing lights approaching through the fog and apply full power to turn off the runway to the left.
KLM captain sees Pan Am and rotates early, striking the tail on the runway for 20 m in an attempt to clear it.
The KLM 747, just airborne at about 140 kt, strikes the upper fuselage of the Pan Am 747 with its fuselage and engines and crashes onto the runway 150 m beyond, exploding in flames.
Fire destroys both aircraft; 583 people die and 61 on the Pan Am aircraft survive. The tower, unable to see the runway, learns of the collision only when the fire is reported.

recommendations.text: Place great emphasis on the importance of exact compliance with instructions and clearances, use standard aeronautical phraseology, and avoid the word 'takeoff' in any ATC clearance other than a takeoff clearance.
recommendations.outcome: ICAO standardised phraseology; 'takeoff' is used only in takeoff clearances and cancellations, and read-back requirements were strengthened.

recommendations.text: Install ground radar at Los Rodeos and other airports where conditions of low visibility and traffic density justify it, and improve taxiway lighting and signage.
recommendations.outcome: Tenerife South airport opened in 1978, relieving Los Rodeos; ground surveillance radar later installed.

recommendations.text: Ensure that the members of a flight crew, whatever their rank, are trained and encouraged to challenge a captain's decision when they have doubts about safety.
recommendations.outcome: The accident became a foundation case for crew resource management training worldwide.

dissent.position: The Netherlands Aviation Safety Board, while accepting the sequence of events, disagreed with the weight given to the KLM captain's actions as the fundamental cause. It emphasised that the mutual misunderstanding created by the ambiguous route clearance, the non-standard phraseology used by the tower, and the simultaneous transmissions that blocked critical messages were of equal importance, and that the KLM crew genuinely believed they had received takeoff clearance.
dissent.topic: probable cause and allocation of responsibility

safety_changes: ICAO standard phraseology reforms: 'takeoff' reserved for takeoff clearances, mandatory read-backs, use of 'departure' for route clearances.
Crew resource management training introduced across the airline industry.
Ground surveillance radar and improved low-visibility taxi procedures at major airports; opening of Tenerife South airport.

notes: The record's aircraft is the KLM 747-206B PH-BUF; the Pan Am aircraft was Boeing 747-121 N736PA. Occupants (644) and fatalities (583) combine both aircraft: KLM 248/248, Pan Am 335 of 396. Serious injuries approximate.

Clock strings are local time; seconds around the collision (about 17:06:50) are approximate reconstructions from the published CVR times and may differ by a few seconds. Earlier times are approximate.
The Spanish report date and title are approximate; Dutch comments were published as an appendix to the Spanish report.
